narratives.narrative: The characteristic is a cry-aloud lifted to the LORD (sense), read as affect (type) — an inner state discharging as voice rather than a reasoned act of will. It is borne by the psalmist (bearer) and located wholly inside the inner state (locus internal:ib-state). Under the triple taunt that there is no salvation for him in God, the operation is the interior going vocal upward: the besieged self answers the verdict of 'no help' by appealing to the only helper, and is answered from the holy hill. Its target is the crying-out itself, welded to the act of crying aloud (coupling). No source (present:false) names a faculty behind the cry — it rises without a stated origin; the seat is none, so this is not a heart- or throat-act but an undifferentiated movement of the whole self; manner is none, and intensity, specifier and effect are all unrecorded — the reading grades no force and books no resulting inner change, so the outcome is carried by the answer, not by an itemised effect. No prohibition attaches: crying aloud is not a forbidden movement. Role marks it a genuine characteristic. Grounding: v4 'I cried aloud to the LORD, and he answered me.'
narratives.story: Voices all around him insist that God will not save him, and in reply the man simply lifts his voice and cries out loud to the LORD — and is answered from God's holy hill. The cry pours straight out of a soul under siege; nothing is said about where inside him it begins or what part of him makes it. Its whole force is just the reaching upward. It is not weighed or measured, and no inner change is tallied afterward; the point is that he cried and was heard. This crying is treated as a real feature of his inner life, and nothing forbids it.
narratives.variation_note: Of the three readings of this cried-item, this is the cry answered directly from the holy hill against a taunt of 'no help' — the accent falls on the immediacy of the reply to a soul told God will not act.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is a call upon the God of righteousness (sense), read as affect (type): the inner state turning Godward as feeling-driven appeal. The psalmist bears it (bearer), and it sits within the inner state (locus internal:ib-state). The operation is a self calling to the God who has already given relief in past distress — appeal grounded in remembered rescue, so the movement runs from memory of a widened narrow place to a present cry for hearing. Its target is appeal, coupled to a call-for-relief. No source (present:false) is named — the cry does not trace to a stated inner faculty; the seat is none, so it is not organ-located; manner is none; and intensity, specifier and effect go unrecorded — the reading does not grade the appeal or book an inner result, leaving the confidence to rest on remembered deliverance rather than a measured effect. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v1 'Answer me when I call, O God of my righteousness! You have given me relief in distress.'
narratives.story: The man calls out to God, and the thing that gives him the nerve to call is memory: God has widened the tight place for him before, so he appeals again now. The cry comes from feeling more than calculation, and it stays entirely inside his own reaching toward God. The words say nothing about where in him the call comes from or how loud it is, and no aftereffect is recorded — the whole weight rests on the God who has rescued him before. It is simply an honest cry for help, and nothing about it is forbidden.
narratives.variation_note: Among the many callings, this one is distinctively anchored in remembered past relief — the appeal leans on a rescue already experienced rather than on assurance of an answer or the pressure of present distress.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is directed morning prayer (sense), read as affect (type): distress shaped into feeling-laden address. The psalmist bears it (bearer), located within the inner state (locus internal:ib-state). The operation is the groaning becoming directed prayer — the king's cry lifted specifically to God, a named King and God, so an inchoate moan is given aim and recipient. Its target is supplication, coupled to praying-to-you. No source (present:false) names an inner origin; the seat is none, so it is not lodged in an organ; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the reading neither grades the prayer nor books a change, so the movement is the shaping itself, not a tallied outcome. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v2 'Give attention to the sound of my cry, my King and my God, for to you do I pray.'
narratives.story: A shapeless groan becomes a real prayer as the man aims it: he takes the raw sound of his distress and directs it to a specific person — his King and his God. What had been only a moan now has a recipient. The text does not say where the prayer rises from inside him or how forceful it is, and it records no result; the moment that matters is the turning of noise into address. This shaping of distress into prayer is a true movement of his inner life.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is the cry of the afflicted (sense), read as affect (type): raw voiced pain. Its bearer is the afflicted (bearer) — not the psalmist but the crushed as a class — and it is located within the inner state (locus internal:ib-state). The operation is that the afflicted cry out and God does not forget their cry: the voiced pain of the crushed is remembered, set against those who forget them. Its target is the crying-out itself, coupled to the afflicted-cry. No source (present:false) is named; the seat is none, so the cry is not organ-located; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the reading books no measured inner effect, so the weight lies in the cry being retained by God rather than in a tallied result. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v12 'he does not forget the cry of the afflicted.'
narratives.story: Here the cry belongs not to one man but to the afflicted as a whole — the crushed and the wronged. Their pain becomes a voice, and the striking thing is that God keeps it: he does not forget the cry of the afflicted, even when everyone else forgets them. Nothing is said about where the cry starts inside them or how loud it grows; what matters is that it reaches God and is held. The voiced pain of the lowly is treated as a real thing that God remembers.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is a refusal to pour out the idolaters' offerings (sense), and crucially it is read as volition (type), not affect — a deliberate act of will, not a feeling. The psalmist bears it (bearer), located within the inner state (locus internal:ib-state). The operation is the self resolving not to pour out their blood drink-offerings or take other gods' names on its lips — a clean break, a deliberate turning from idolatry so total the interior will not even name the rival gods. Its target is refusal-of-idols, coupled to refuse-idolatry. No source (present:false) names an inner faculty; the seat is none, so the resolve is not organ-located; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the will is stated without graded force or booked outcome. Notably no prohibition dimension is recorded (present:false) even though the content is itself a self-imposed refusal — the negation lives in the operation, not in a prohibition tag. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v4 'their drink offerings of blood I will not pour out or take their names on my lips.'
narratives.story: Unlike the cries around it, this is an act of the will, not a wave of feeling: the man decides he will have nothing to do with other gods. He refuses to pour out their offerings, and he will not even let their names cross his lips — a clean, total break. The passage does not locate this resolve in any part of him or measure its strength; it simply states the decision. Interestingly, though the act is a refusal, it is not framed as a rule he is obeying — the 'no' is the movement itself, a deliberate turning of the inner self away from idolatry.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is a plea from guileless lips (sense), read as affect (type). The psalmist bears it (bearer), located within the inner state (locus internal:ib-state). The operation is the self asking God to hear a just cause from lips free of deceit — an appeal staked on its own honesty, so the movement grounds the right to be heard in the truthfulness of its speech. Its target is honest-appeal, coupled to a plea-no-deceit. No source (present:false) names an inner origin; the seat is none, so the prayer is not organ-located despite its mention of lips — the reading keeps it a whole-self movement, not a mouth-act; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — no graded force, no booked result, the confidence resting on integrity rather than a measured outcome. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v1 'Hear a just cause, O LORD... give ear to my prayer from lips free of deceit.'
narratives.story: The man asks God to listen, and the ground he stands on is his own honesty: his lips are free of deceit, so he believes his prayer deserves a hearing. The appeal is driven by feeling and stays inside his reaching toward God. Even though he speaks of his lips, the prayer is not pinned to his mouth as an organ — it is the whole honest self appealing. No strength is measured and no outcome is recorded; the point is a clean plea from a truthful heart.
narratives.variation_note: Among the prayer-items this one is distinctive in staking its plea on the psalmist's own truthfulness — the appeal's ground is the integrity of his speech, not (as elsewhere) God's steadfast love or the pressure of enemies.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is a call made confident of an answer (sense), read as affect (type). The psalmist bears it (bearer), located within the inner state (locus internal:ib-state). The operation is the self calling upon God confident he will answer — appeal made in assurance, so the movement is not a cry into silence but a call to a God certain to incline his ear. Its target is confident-calling, coupled to a call-for-answer. No source (present:false) is named; the seat is none, so it is not organ-located; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the reading does not grade the confidence or book a result, the certainty carried in the operation itself. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v6 'I call upon you, for you will answer me, O God.'
narratives.story: This call is quietly sure of itself: the man calls on God precisely because he knows God will answer him. It is not a desperate shout into the dark but a confident appeal to a God certain to bend his ear. Nothing is said about where the call rises from or how loud it is, and no result is tallied — the assurance is built into the calling itself. That settled confidence is treated as a real trait of his inner life.
narratives.variation_note: Distinctive among the callings for its note of assurance — the appeal is made in the certainty of being answered, contrasting with the dread-of-silence or unanswered cries elsewhere.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is the plea 'keep me as the apple of your eye' (sense), read as affect (type). The psalmist bears it (bearer), located within the inner state (locus internal:ib-state). The operation is the self asking to be guarded as the pupil of the eye and hidden in the shadow of God's wings — a longing for the most intimate, close-in protection, to be as precious and guarded as the eye's own pupil. Its target is intimate-refuge-longing, coupled to the apple-of-eye image. No source (present:false) names an inner origin; the seat is none, so the longing is not organ-located; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the reading does not grade the yearning or book a result, the whole weight lying in the tenderness of the request. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v8 'Keep me as the apple of your eye; hide me in the shadow of your wings.'
narratives.story: This is prayer as tender longing: the man asks to be guarded the way the eye guards its own pupil, and to be hidden under the shadow of God's wings. He is reaching for the closest, most intimate kind of protection — to be that precious to God. The passage does not measure how strong the yearning is or record any answer; the whole point is the tenderness of the asking. That longing to be cherished and kept safe is a real movement of his inner life.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is 'call and be saved' (sense), read as affect (type). The psalmist bears it (bearer), located within the inner state (locus internal:ib-state). The operation is the self calling on the LORD, who is worthy of praise, and being saved from its enemies — the summary confidence that states the whole pattern in miniature: to call is to be delivered. Its target is calling, coupled to call-and-saved. No source (present:false) is named; the seat is none, so it is not organ-located; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the deliverance sits in the operation as the pattern, not as a separately booked effect. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v3 'I call upon the LORD, who is worthy to be praised, and I am saved from my enemies.'
narratives.story: This calling is a whole story told in one line: he calls on the LORD, and he is saved. It is the settled pattern of his life stated as a summary — to cry to God is to be rescued. Nothing is said about the source or loudness of the call, and the salvation is folded straight into the act of calling rather than listed as a separate outcome. This confident habit of calling and being delivered is treated as a real feature of who he is.
narratives.variation_note: This is the summary, confident statement of the whole call-and-rescue pattern; it differs from the very next reading (Psa 18:6), which narrows to the specific cry from the snares of death.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is a cry in distress (sense), read as affect (type). The psalmist bears it (bearer), located within the inner state (locus internal:ib-state). The operation is that, in distress with the cords of death around it, the self calls and cries, and its cry reaches God's ears — the specific cry from the snares of death that triggers the theophany. Its target is distress-cry, coupled to cry-in-distress. No source (present:false) is named; the seat is none, so it is not organ-located; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the reading does not grade the cry, and the answering upheaval (the earth reeling) is not booked as an itemised inner effect but follows the cry in the narrative. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v6 'In my distress I called upon the LORD... my cry to him reached his ears.'
narratives.story: Here the calling is at its rawest: with the ropes of death wound around him, he cries out, and his cry travels all the way to God's ears. This is the concrete, desperate cry from the trap of death — and in the psalm it is what sets God's rescue in motion. The text does not measure how loud or intense it is; it simply shows the cry reaching God. That cry from the edge of death is a genuine movement of his inner life.
narratives.variation_note: Distinct from the summary call of Psa 18:3: this is the specific, concrete cry from the snares of death — the cry that reaches God's ears and triggers the theophany that follows.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is a cry by day that receives no answer (sense), read as affect (type). The psalmist bears it (bearer), located within the inner state (locus internal:ib-state). The operation is the self crying by day and by night and finding no answer, no rest — persistence into silence. Read without valence bias, this is the dark movement: the cry that keeps going into an unbroken silence, refused the very hearing that elsewhere defines the item. Its target is unanswered-crying, coupled to cry-no-answer. No source (present:false) is named; the seat is none, so it is not organ-located; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — and here the absence of a booked effect is itself telling: no result is registered because none comes, the silence standing where an answer would. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v2 'O my God, I cry by day, but you do not answer, and by night, but I find no rest.'
narratives.story: This is the cry that gets no reply. Day and night he calls, and still there is only silence and no rest — the calling wears on into an emptiness that never answers back. It is the same act of crying out, but here it meets nothing, and that unanswered silence is the whole point. Nothing is recorded as coming of it, because nothing does. The passage lets this stand exactly as it is: a real, faithful cry that, for now, goes unheard.
narratives.variation_note: Among the cry-items this is the dark reading — the same crying, but persisted into unbroken silence with no answer; it holds open the possibility that the cry meets no reply, over against the answered cries elsewhere.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is 'the fathers cried and were not shamed' (sense), read as affect (type). Its bearer is the fathers (bearer) — the ancestors, not the psalmist — and it is located within the inner state (locus internal:ib-state). The operation is that to God the fathers cried and were rescued; they trusted and were not put to shame — a remembered layer of ancestral ground, the cry answered and shame averted. Its target is remembered-rescue, coupled to fathers-not-shamed. No source (present:false) is named; the seat is none, so it is not organ-located; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the reading books no separate effect, the rescue folded into the remembered cry. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v5 'To you they cried and were rescued; in you they trusted and were not put to shame.'
narratives.story: This cry belongs to the ancestors, not the psalmist himself. He remembers how the fathers cried out to God and were rescued, trusted him and were never put to shame. He brings up their answered cries precisely because they are the very things he now feels he lacks. Nothing is said about where their cry came from or how strong it was; the memory is simply that they cried and God came through. That remembered rescue is held up as a real ground for hope.
narratives.variation_note: Of the three readings of this cried-item, this one places the accent on the cry answered and shame averted in the fathers' generation — the collective, remembered rescue, contrasting the psalmist's present sense of being unanswered.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is a cry aloud for a hearing (sense), read as affect (type). The psalmist bears it (bearer), located within the inner state (locus internal:ib-state). The operation is the self crying aloud and asking God to be gracious and answer — the appeal for attention, the turn from the psalm's earlier confidence to urgent petition. Its target is the crying-out itself, coupled to cry-aloud. No source (present:false) is named; the seat is none, so it is not organ-located; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the reading grades no force and books no result, the urgency carried by the operation. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v7 'Hear, O LORD, when I cry aloud; be gracious to me and answer me.'
narratives.story: After all his earlier confidence, the man suddenly turns urgent: hear me, be gracious, answer me. He lifts his voice and cries aloud, asking God to pay attention. It is a swing from steadiness to pressing need. The passage does not say where the cry rises from or how loud it grows, and records no reply here; the moment is the lifted, pleading voice itself. That urgent cry for a hearing is a real movement of his inner life.
narratives.variation_note: Distinctive for its swing from confidence to urgency within the same psalm — the crying here is the turn from steady assurance to pressing petition for a hearing.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is a call 'lest you be silent' (sense), read as affect (type). The psalmist bears it (bearer), located within the inner state (locus internal:ib-state). The operation is the self calling to its rock, begging God not to be deaf, lest it become like those who go down to the pit — a cry that dreads divine silence, fearing not the enemies but God's non-answer, for silence from God would be death. Its target is dread-of-silence, coupled to call-be-not-deaf. No source (present:false) is named; the seat is none, so it is not organ-located; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the dread lives in the operation, not a booked effect. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v1 'To you, O LORD, I call; my rock, be not deaf to me, lest... I become like those who go down to the pit.'
narratives.story: What terrifies this man is not his enemies but the thought that God might stay silent. He calls to his rock and begs him not to be deaf, because if God does not answer he is as good as dead, sinking into the pit. The whole cry is shot through with the fear of a God who does not reply. The passage does not measure the fear or record an answer; the movement is the calling that dreads silence. That dread is treated as a genuine part of his inner life.
narratives.variation_note: Distinctive among the callings for its object of dread: not the enemy but God's own silence — to be unanswered would be death, so the call is driven by fear of divine deafness.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is a cry that pleads for mercy (sense), read as affect (type). The psalmist bears it (bearer), located within the inner state (locus internal:ib-state). The operation is that, out of dismay when God hid his face, the self cries to the LORD and pleads for mercy — the appeal from the edge of the pit, the shaken interior lifting a cry. Its target is pleading, coupled to cry-and-plead. No source (present:false) is named; the seat is none, so it is not organ-located; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the reading grades no force and books no result, the turn from dismay to petition carried in the operation. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v8 'To you, O LORD, I cry, and to the Lord I plead for mercy.'
narratives.story: God had hidden his face, and the man was thrown into dismay — and out of that shaken state he cries and begs for mercy. This is the appeal from the very edge of the pit, a rattled soul lifting its voice. The passage does not say how loud the cry is or record its answer; the movement is the turn from dismay to pleading. That crying for mercy from a shaken heart is a real feature of his inner life.
narratives.variation_note: Distinctive for rising out of dismay at God's hidden face — the cry is the turn from a shaken, destabilised state into direct petition for mercy.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is 'I cried for help, and you healed me' (sense), read as affect (type). The psalmist bears it (bearer), located within the inner state (locus internal:ib-state). The operation is the self crying to God for help and being healed — the appeal answered with restoration, stating the whole pattern: the cry met by healing. Its target is crying-answered, coupled to cried-and-healed. No source (present:false) is named; the seat is none, so it is not organ-located; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the healing is folded into the operation as the answered cry, not booked as a separate effect. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v2 'O LORD my God, I cried to you for help, and you have healed me.'
narratives.story: This is the whole shape of prayer in a single line: he cried to God for help, and God healed him. The cry and its answer come together — reach out in need, and be restored. The passage does not describe where the cry came from or how strong it was, and it does not list the healing as a separate result; the healing simply is the cry answered. That pattern of crying and being healed is held up as a real trait of his life.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is 'in my alarm I said, I am cut off' (sense), and it is read as state (type), not affect — a condition of panic the self was in, not a feeling it directed. The psalmist bears it (bearer), located within the inner state (locus internal:ib-state). The operation is the self recalling that in its alarm it thought it was cut off from God's sight — yet God heard when it cried: panic corrected by being heard, a confession that the interior had despaired of God's attention and was proved wrong. Its target is panic-corrected, coupled to cut-off-yet-heard. No source (present:false) is named; the seat is none, so the alarm is not organ-located; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the reading does not grade the panic, and the correction lies in the operation, not a booked effect. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v22 'I had said in my alarm, I am cut off from your sight. But you heard the voice of my pleas.'
narratives.story: This is a confession of a false alarm. In a moment of panic the man had decided he was completely cut off from God's sight — and he was wrong, because God heard him after all. It is not a feeling he aimed at God but a state of fright he fell into, which the outcome then corrected. The passage does not measure how deep the panic was; it simply shows the man admitting he had despaired too soon. That honest report of a corrected panic is treated as a real part of his inner life.
narratives.variation_note: Of the two alarm readings, this one ends in correction: the panic that thought itself cut off is proved wrong by being heard, whereas the other (Psa 116:11) hardens into distrust of all men.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is 'let the godly pray while you may be found' (sense), read as volition (type), not affect — a counselled act of will, an exhortation to a deliberate movement. Its bearer is the godly (bearer) as a class, and it is located within the inner state (locus internal:ib-state). The operation is that everyone who is godly should offer prayer at a time when God may be found, safe from the rush of great waters — the urgency of seeking while there is time, the lesson that the interior should seek God now, in the window of grace, before the flood. Its target is timely-prayer, coupled to pray-while-found. No source (present:false) is named; the seat is none, so it is not organ-located; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the will is counselled without graded force or booked result. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v6 'let everyone who is godly offer prayer to you at a time when you may be found.'
narratives.story: Out of his own experience of forgiveness the man draws a lesson for everyone who wants to be godly: pray now, while God can still be found, before the flood comes. This is not a wave of feeling but a piece of hard-won counsel — a call to act deliberately and not miss the window of grace. The passage does not measure the urgency or record a result; it simply presses the timing. Seeking God in time is held up as a wise and real movement of the inner life.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is 'this poor man cried and was heard' (sense), read as affect (type). Its bearer is the poor man (bearer) — the lowly one, offered as an example — located within the inner state (locus internal:ib-state). The operation is that this poor man cried, and the LORD heard and saved him from all his troubles — the cry of the lowly answered, poverty of estate no barrier to being heard. Its target is crying-answered, coupled to poor-man-cried. No source (present:false) is named; the seat is none, so it is not organ-located; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the salvation is folded into the answered cry, not a separately booked effect. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v6 'This poor man cried, and the LORD heard him and saved him out of all his troubles.'
narratives.story: Here the one who cries is a poor man, held up as proof of something: he cried, and the LORD heard him and pulled him out of all his troubles. The point is that being lowly and without means is no obstacle to being heard — the humblest cry still reaches God. The passage does not describe how loud or intense the cry was, and it does not separate out the rescue; the rescue simply is the cry answered. That answered cry of the lowly is treated as a real and encouraging feature of the inner life.
narratives.variation_note: Of the three readings of this cried-item, this one foregrounds lowliness: the crier is a poor man, and the finding is that poverty is no barrier to being heard and saved.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is 'hold not your peace at my tears' (sense), read as affect (type). The psalmist bears it (bearer), located within the inner state (locus internal:ib-state). The operation is the self asking God to hear its prayer and cry and not to be silent at its tears, for it is a sojourner and guest with him — crying as a passing guest, a plea from transience, the interior weeping as a fleeting visitor asking the eternal host not to stay silent. Its target is sojourner-tears, coupled to cry-as-sojourner. No source (present:false) is named; the seat is none, so it is not organ-located; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the reading grades no force and books no result, the plea resting on transience rather than a measured effect. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v12 'Hear my prayer... hold not your peace at my tears! For I am a sojourner with you, a guest.'
narratives.story: The man weeps and begs God not to stay silent at his tears — and the reason he gives is his own smallness: he is only a passing guest, a stranger stopping briefly with God. He asks the eternal host to notice the tears of a visitor who will soon be gone. The passage does not measure the weeping or record an answer; the whole appeal leans on how fleeting his life is. That cry of a transient soul is a real movement of his inner life.
narratives.variation_note: Of the two readings of this cry-item, this one grounds the plea in transience — the crier weeps as a passing guest and stranger, distinct from the plain 'let my cry come to you' of Psa 102:1.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is the startling plea 'look away, that I may smile again' (sense), read as affect (type). The psalmist bears it (bearer), located within the inner state (locus internal:ib-state). The operation is the self asking God to look away from it, that it may smile again before it departs and is no more — a poignant, almost desperate request for the gaze of judgment to relent, the interior asking the scrutinising God to ease off so it can know one last gladness before death. Read without valence bias, this is a movement against expectation: not 'turn to me' but 'turn from me.' Its target is plea-for-respite, coupled to look-away. No source (present:false) is named; the seat is none, so it is not organ-located; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the reading books no result, the anguish carried by the operation. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v13 'Look away from me, that I may smile again, before I depart and am no more!'
narratives.story: This prayer runs backward from what we expect: instead of asking God to look at him, the man begs God to look away. God's searching gaze has become so crushing that he pleads for it to ease off, just long enough to smile once more before he dies and is gone. It is a raw, almost shocking request. The passage does not measure the desperation or record any answer; it lets the strange plea stand. That longing for God's scrutiny to relent is reported honestly as a real movement of the inner life.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is prayer (tefillah) (sense), and unusually it is read as status (type) rather than an act — a standing condition rather than a discrete movement. Its bearer is David (bearer), and it is oriented outward to God (locus external:god), its target the God of my life. Tellingly, the operation is none: no operation-event is recorded, because here prayer is not a cry launched in a moment but a companion presence — at night God's song is with the sufferer, a prayer sustained by the daytime steadfast love (its source: grounded by the chesed God commands by day). Its manner is at night, a song; its coupling is none, so it is not welded to another act but stands alone as a nocturnal song-prayer. No seat (none) locates it in an organ; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — no graded force, no booked outcome, the prayer existing as a state rather than an event with a result. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v8 'at night his song is with me, a prayer to the God of my life.'
narratives.story: For this sufferer, prayer is less a sudden cry than a steady companion. By day God commands his steadfast love, and by night that love turns into a song — a prayer that simply keeps him company in the dark, directed to the God who is his very life. The passage does not describe an act of crying out here; the prayer is more a quiet, ongoing state than a single event. Nothing is measured and no result is tallied. This night-long, song-shaped prayer is treated as a real feature of his inner life.
narratives.variation_note: Uniquely among the prayer-items, this reading is a standing state, not an act: prayer as a night-song companioning the sufferer, sustained by God's daytime love — no discrete crying-out is recorded.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is a call in the sense of naming — 'they called lands by their own names' (sense), read as action (type). Its bearer is the wealthy (bearer), and here, against the family's Godward pattern, the movement is turned inward on the self: the locus is internal:ib-state, and the coupling is none — this calling is welded to nothing beyond the self. Read without valence bias, this is the descent form of the item: the operation is the naming of estates after oneself, the vain bid for lasting memory, though the grave is the only home that endures. Its target is lands, called by their own names. No source (present:false) is named — the drive for self-perpetuation is stated without a traced inner origin; no seat (none) locates it; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — no graded force, and pointedly no lasting effect, since the reading elsewhere insists the memory perishes. No prohibition attaches, though the movement is futile. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v11 'though they called lands by their own names.'
narratives.story: This 'calling' is not prayer at all — it is the rich naming their estates after themselves, trying to make their names last forever. It is the same word turned in the wrong direction: instead of calling on God, they call the world after themselves, grasping at a memory the grave will erase. Nothing is said about what drives this hunger from the inside; it simply names it. And the striking silence is that no lasting result comes of it — the memory dies with them. The passage reports this self-directed craving for permanence plainly, as a real and futile movement of the inner life.
narratives.variation_note: The lone descent-reading among the callings: here 'call' means naming estates after oneself for lasting memory — turned inward on the self, coupled to nothing beyond it, and futile, over against the Godward callings elsewhere.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is a call upon God (sense), read as action (type). Its bearer is the worshipper (bearer), oriented outward to God (locus external:god), its target God in the day of trouble. The operation is calling upon God, and its source is God's own promise to answer: it is a call answered by God's deliverance. Its manner is in the day of trouble, and its coupling is that it issues in glorifying God — the movement runs call, then rescue, then praise, a full cycle of dependent trust. No seat (none) locates it in an organ; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the deliverance and glorifying live in the operation and coupling, not as a separately booked effect. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v15 'call upon me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me.'
narratives.story: This is what real worship looks like: in the day of trouble, call on God, and he will rescue you — and then you will give him the glory. The whole cycle is here — cry out, be delivered, give thanks — and God himself invites it. The call is a deliberate act, aimed squarely at God, resting on his promise to answer. The passage does not measure it or list the rescue as a separate item; the deliverance and the praise are built into the calling itself. This dependent, God-glorifying prayer is held up as a true feature of the inner life.
narratives.variation_note: Distinctive for God himself commanding the call and naming its outcome: this reading runs the full cycle of call, deliverance, and glorifying God, whereas most callings state only the appeal.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is a plea to be purged — chata in its rare privative sense, to de-sin or un-sin (sense), read as action (type). Its bearer is the penitent, longing to be purged (bearer), and it is located within the inner state (locus internal:ib-state). The operation is the self pleading to be purged, de-sinned, washed whiter than snow — the purity-hunger of the psalm renewed. Its manner is with hyssop, the ritual-deep cleansing. Strikingly, the target is none: the movement has no external object, turning wholly in upon the self to be cleansed. Its coupling is to 'I shall be clean' / whiter than snow. No source (present:false) is named; no seat (none) locates it; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the reading books no measured result, the longed-for cleanness carried in the coupling. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v7 'Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean.'
narratives.story: This is prayer as a hunger to be made clean. The penitent begs God to scrub the sin out of him, to un-sin him as with the ceremonial hyssop, until he is whiter than snow. Notice there is no outward object here at all — the whole force of the plea turns inward, on his own defiled self longing to be pure. The passage does not measure the longing or record the result; it simply pairs the plea with the hope of being clean. That deep hunger for purity is treated as a genuine movement of his inner life.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is calling upon God (sense), read as action (type), but here in its negated, absent form: the bearer is the evildoers who do not (bearer). Read without valence bias, this is the dark reading — the operation is a call refused, the prayerlessness that marks the godless, the practical expression of 'there is no God' (v1): they neither seek nor invoke him. Its target is God, and its coupling is with devouring God's people — the refusal to call runs alongside preying on the vulnerable. It is oriented (in its negation) toward God (locus external:god). No source (present:false) is named; no seat (none) locates it; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the silence of the effect matches the silence of their prayer. No prohibition dimension is recorded, though the refusal is itself a moral failure. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v4 'and do not call upon God.'
narratives.story: This reading shows the trait by its absence: the evildoers do not call on God at all. Their prayerlessness is the living proof of their creed that there is no God — they never seek him or cry to him, and meanwhile they devour his people like bread. The passage does not trace what stops them inside or measure anything; it simply notes the empty place where prayer should be. That refusal to call on God is reported honestly as a real and telling feature of the godless inner life.
narratives.variation_note: The negated calling among the God-callers: here the item appears as a refusal — the godless do not call on God — set against those whose defining movement is precisely to call.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is prayer (tefillah) — 'hear my prayer' (sense), read as action (type). The psalmist (David) bears it (bearer), oriented outward to God (locus external:god), its target God. The operation is to pray, to cry out; its source is an appeal to God's name and might to save and vindicate (v1) — trust voiced as petition. Here, uncommonly, a seat is given: the mouth (words of my mouth), so this prayer is anchored in the organ of speech, spoken aloud (manner: aloud, the words of his mouth). Its coupling is none — the prayer stands as the whole psalm's engine, not welded to another act. Intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — no graded force, no booked outcome, the petition leaning on God's name rather than a measured result. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v2 'O God, hear my prayer; give ear to the words of my mouth.'
narratives.story: An endangered man throws himself on God in prayer, and this prayer is spoken out loud — the words of his mouth, lifted for God to hear. What he leans on is God's own name and power to save and clear his name. It is a deliberate act, aimed straight at God, and it drives the whole psalm. The passage does not measure it or record its result; the trust simply becomes a spoken petition. That out-loud casting of himself on God is a real movement of his inner life.
narratives.variation_note: Distinctive among the prayer-items for being explicitly seated in the mouth and spoken aloud, and for leaning on God's name and might — trust voiced as the psalm's driving petition.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is prayer (tefillah) — 'give ear to my prayer' (sense), read as action (type). The psalmist bears it (bearer), oriented outward to God (locus external:god), its target God. The operation is to pray, to cry out; its source is the asking that God give ear and not hide himself (v1), and its manner is begging God not to hide himself — a prayer shadowed by the dread of divine concealment. Its coupling is with the plea for grace (supplication). No seat (none) locates it in an organ; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — no graded force, no booked result, the whole desperate psalm anchored in this opening cry. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v1 'Give ear to my prayer, O God, and hide not yourself from my plea.'
narratives.story: A man in extremity begins by begging God simply to listen — and, more, not to hide from him. The fear running underneath is that God might turn his face away, so the prayer pleads for attention as much as for help. It is a deliberate cry, aimed at God, and it opens the whole desperate psalm that follows. The passage does not measure the prayer or record an answer; it captures the opening plea itself. That dread-shadowed appeal for God's ear is a real movement of the inner life.
narratives.variation_note: Distinctive for its dread of God's concealment: the prayer's manner is begging God not to hide himself, giving this appeal an anxious edge the more confident prayers lack.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is complaint or lament (siach) — 'restless in my complaint' (sense), read as action (type). The psalmist bears it (bearer), oriented outward to God (locus external:god), its target God. The operation is to pour out complaint — the voicing of inner distress before God — and its manner is restlessly, an agitation that cannot keep still. Its coupling is that the complaint is renewed evening, morning and noon (v17), grief kept up on a rhythm. No source (present:false) is named; no seat (none) locates it; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the reading books no measured outcome, the distress carried in the outpouring itself. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v2 'restless in my complaint.'
narratives.story: This man cannot sit still with his pain, so he pours it out to God as a running complaint. It is grief given words, spoken aloud and kept up morning, noon, and night. The complaint is a deliberate act, aimed at God, not just a private brooding. The passage does not measure how heavy it is or record a reply; the movement is simply the restless emptying of distress before God. That voiced, agitated lament is treated as a real feature of his inner life.
narratives.variation_note: Of this complaint-item's readings, this one accents restlessness and the rhythm of renewal (evening, morning, noon), whereas the parallel at Psa 64:1 is driven by dread of the enemy and Psa 102:1 is grief poured out in weakness.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is a call upon God — 'but I call to God' (sense), read as action (type). The psalmist bears it (bearer), oriented outward to God (locus external:god), its target God. The operation is the decisive turn from dread to trust: surrounded by treachery, the self calls to God, its one recourse; its source is the confidence that the LORD will save him (v16). Its coupling is the calling that the complaint sustains (v17), so the persistent lament feeds a steady calling. No seat (none) locates it; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the salvation lives in the source, not a booked effect. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v16 'But I call to God, and the LORD will save me.'
narratives.story: Betrayed and surrounded by treachery, the man makes his choice: 'But I call to God.' It is the decisive turn from dread to trust — his one true recourse against the deceit around him — and he is sure the LORD will save him. His ongoing complaint feeds this steady calling rather than replacing it. The passage does not measure the call or record the rescue as a separate event; the certainty of being saved is simply built in. That resolute cry of the betrayed is a real movement of his inner life.
narratives.variation_note: Distinctive as the psalm's hinge from dread to trust: the calling here is the deliberate 'but I' recourse of the betrayed, sustained by the ongoing complaint and confident of rescue.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is complaint or musing (siach) — 'I utter my complaint' (sense), read as action (type). Note this is a distinct lament-item from the siach of v2, and the difference is preserved: here the accent is persistent, rhythmed prayer. The psalmist bears it (bearer), oriented outward to God (locus external:god), its target God. The operation is to pour out complaint; its source is that God hears the psalmist's voice (v17), and its manner is evening, morning and at noon. Its coupling is with moaning, renewing the complaint of v2 — grief that does not despair but keeps addressing God. No seat (none) locates it; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the reading books no measured result, the hearing carried by the source. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v17 'Evening and morning and at noon I utter my complaint and moan.'
narratives.story: Three times a day — evening, morning, and noon — the man pours out his complaint to God and moans his grief aloud. This is lament turned into a discipline, kept up on a rhythm, and the quiet confidence under it is that God actually hears his voice. It is grief that keeps speaking to God rather than sinking into despair. The passage does not measure the sorrow or list a result; it simply shows the complaint repeated and heard. That steady, rhythmed lament is a real feature of his inner life.
narratives.variation_note: Though it echoes the complaint of v2, this is a distinct lament-item: its finding is persistence and rhythm (thrice daily) coupled with the assurance that God hears — grief that keeps addressing God rather than despairing.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is a call — 'in the day when I call' (sense), read as action (type). The psalmist bears it (bearer), oriented outward to God (locus external:god), its target God. The operation is calling upon God with the confident expectation that the enemies will turn back in the day he calls — prayer as effective recourse. Its coupling is with the knowledge that God is for him: the certainty that his cry moves God to act. No source (present:false) is named as an inner origin; no seat (none) locates it; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the rout of the enemies lives in the operation, not a separately booked effect. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v9 'my enemies will turn back in the day when I call.'
narratives.story: This man is sure his prayer works: the very day he calls, his enemies will fall back. Under the confidence lies a settled conviction — God is on his side. So calling on God is not a shot in the dark but a move he trusts to shift the battle. The passage does not measure the call or list the enemies' retreat as a separate result; the certainty is simply that his cry moves God to act. That confident recourse to prayer is a real feature of his inner life.
narratives.variation_note: Distinctive for its confidence that the call itself routs the enemy — the appeal rests on the knowledge that God is for him, so calling is treated as effective, not merely hopeful.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is to cry out or call (qara) — 'I cry out to God Most High' (sense), read as action (type). The psalmist bears it (bearer), oriented outward to God (locus external:god), its target God Most High. The operation is crying out and calling to the Most High; its source is God who fulfils his purpose for him and sends his love to save (v2-3) — a plea that already trusts the outcome. Its coupling is none, so the cry stands alone, resting only on God's committed purpose. No seat (none) locates it; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the assured outcome lives in the source, not a booked effect. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v2 'I cry out to God Most High, to God who fulfils his purpose for me.'
narratives.story: Hiding in a cave, the man cries out to God Most High — and the remarkable thing is his confidence: he cries to the God who fulfils his purpose for him and sends his love to rescue. So even the cry of distress already trusts the ending. It is a deliberate reach upward, resting on nothing but God's settled commitment to him. The passage does not measure the cry or record the rescue separately; the assurance is built into whom he cries to. That trusting cry from the cave is a real movement of his inner life.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is a ringing cry (rinnah) — 'hear my cry' (sense), read as action (type). The psalmist bears it (bearer), oriented outward to God (locus external:god), its target God. The operation is to cry out — the earnest, ringing call of a soul reaching toward God — and its source is the psalmist's own asking that God would hear it (v1). Its coupling is with the prayer, the cry twinned with settled petition. No seat (none) locates it; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — no graded force, no booked result, the appeal resting on God's hearing. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v1 'Hear my cry, O God.'
narratives.story: From the ends of the earth the man sends up a ringing cry and begs God to hear it. It is the earnest, high call of a soul stretching toward God, and it comes paired with his steadier prayer. The whole appeal leans on one thing: that God would actually listen. The passage does not measure how loud or intense it is or record a reply; the movement is the cry lifted for God's ear. That ringing appeal is a real feature of his inner life.
narratives.variation_note: Of this cry-item's readings, this one is twinned with the prayer as the opening appeal from the ends of the earth, distinct from the persistent night-cry of Psa 88:2 and the word-seeking cries of Psalm 119.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is prayer (tefillah) — 'listen to my prayer' (sense), read as action (type). The psalmist bears it (bearer), oriented outward to God (locus external:god), its target God. The operation is to pray — the settled appeal lifted to God — and its source is the asking that God would listen to it (v1). Its coupling is with the cry, the prayer voiced in the calling of v2, so prayer and cry work as one recourse. No seat (none) locates it; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — no graded force, no booked outcome, the whole recourse resting on God's attention. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v1 'listen to my prayer.'
narratives.story: Alongside his ringing cry, the man asks God to listen to his prayer — the steadier twin of the same appeal. Cry and prayer belong together here as his one recourse in distress. What he asks for is simply God's attention. The passage does not measure the prayer or record an answer; the movement is the settled petition lifted to God. That paired cry-and-prayer is a real feature of his inner life.
narratives.variation_note: Twinned with the cry of v1: this reading is the settled-prayer half of the same appeal, distinguished by its steadier register beside the ringing rinnah-cry.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is a call — 'from the end of the earth I call to you' (sense), read as action (type). The psalmist bears it (bearer), oriented outward to God (locus external:god), its target God. The operation is calling upon God, and its striking manner is from the end of the earth, with the heart fainting — the reach of prayer across every distance of body or soul. Its coupling reframes the cry and prayer as a calling from afar. No source (present:false) is named as an inner origin; no seat (none) locates it; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — no graded force, no booked result, the finding lying in prayer's reach when the heart fails. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v2 'from the end of the earth I call to you when my heart is faint.'
narratives.story: No distance is too great for this call: from the farthest edge of the earth — and the farthest edge of himself, his heart fainting — the man still calls to God. The point is prayer's reach: even when the heart is giving out and God feels impossibly far, the cry still goes up. The passage does not measure the faintness or record a reply; the movement is the calling that crosses every distance. That far-flung cry when strength fails is a real feature of his inner life.
narratives.variation_note: Distinctive for the theme of distance: this calling is lifted 'from the end of the earth' with a fainting heart — its finding is prayer's reach across every remoteness of body or soul.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is complaint or lament (siach) — 'hear my voice in my complaint' (sense), read as action (type). The psalmist bears it (bearer), oriented outward to God (locus external:god), its target God. The operation is to pour out complaint — voiced distress laid before God — and its source is the asking that God hear and preserve his life (v1). Its coupling is that it is driven by dread of the enemy: prayer as recourse against secret, unseen plots. No seat (none) locates it; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — no graded force, no booked result, the appeal resting on God's protection. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v1 'Hear my voice, O God, in my complaint.'
narratives.story: Beset by secret enemies, the man pours out his complaint to God and asks to be heard and kept alive. What drives the lament is dread — the fear of hidden plots he cannot see or fight. So prayer becomes his defence: he lays the fear before God and asks for protection. The passage does not measure the dread or record a rescue; the movement is the voiced complaint offered against unseen danger. That fear-driven lament is a real feature of his inner life.
narratives.variation_note: Of this complaint-item's readings, this one is driven by dread of secret enemies and seeks preservation of life — prayer as defence against unseen plots, distinct from the rhythmed restlessness of Psa 55:2 and the weakness of Psa 102:1.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is prayer (tefillah) — 'O you who hear prayer' (sense), read as action (type). Its bearer is all who pray (bearer), for the reading widens beyond the psalmist to humanity as such; it is oriented outward to God (locus external:god), its target the God who hears prayer. The operation is to pray, offered to the God who hears it; its coupling is with all flesh coming to God — the universal recourse of humanity. No source (present:false) is named; no seat (none) locates it; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — no graded force, no booked result, the confidence lying in God's character as the prayer-hearer. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v2 'O you who hear prayer, to you shall all flesh come.'
narratives.story: Here prayer belongs to everyone: God is the one who hears prayer, and so all flesh will come to him. The reading lifts its eyes from one man to the whole human race, whose common recourse is to bring their prayers to a God who listens. The passage does not measure any single prayer or record a specific answer; the confidence rests on who God is — the prayer-hearer. That universal turning of humanity toward God in prayer is treated as a real feature of the inner life.
narratives.variation_note: Uniquely universal among the prayer-items: the bearer is all who pray, and the finding is that God's identity as the prayer-hearer draws all flesh to him, rather than one man's particular appeal.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is to cry or call (qara) — 'I cried to him with my mouth' (sense), read as action (type). The psalmist bears it (bearer), oriented outward to God (locus external:god), its target God. The operation is crying and calling to God, the prayer that God answered; here a seat is given — the mouth — so the cry is anchored in the organ of speech, and its manner is high praise on his tongue, the cry joined to praise. Its coupling is with that high praise on the tongue. No source (present:false) names an inner origin; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the answer (v19) sits in the operation as testimony, not a separately booked effect. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v17 'I cried to him with my mouth.'
narratives.story: This is a testimony after the fact: 'I cried to him with my mouth' — and God listened. The cry came out on his lips, joined to high praise on his tongue, so crying and praising rose together. The whole point is that he called and God heard him. The passage does not trace where the cry began inside him or measure it, and it folds the answer straight into the testimony. That spoken cry, wedded to praise and answered by God, is a real feature of his inner life.
narratives.variation_note: Of the three readings of this cried-item, this one is a testimony seated in the mouth and joined to praise on the tongue — the cry recalled as already answered, distinct from the fresh cries of Psalms 3 and 34.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is prayer (tefillah) — 'he has attended to the voice of my prayer' (sense), read as action (type). The psalmist bears it (bearer), oriented outward to God (locus external:god), its target God. The operation is to pray, here recalled as answered; its source is the prayer which God has listened to and attended (v19). Its coupling is that same attended prayer — the climax of the testimony, proof that God did not reject him. No seat (none) locates it; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the outcome (God's attention) lives in the source, not a separately booked effect. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v19 'God has listened; he has attended to the voice of my prayer.'
narratives.story: This is the high point of the man's testimony: God has actually listened; he attended to the voice of his prayer. The prayer is looked back on as already answered — the proof that God did not turn him away. The passage does not measure the prayer itself; its whole weight is that God heard it. That answered prayer, recalled as the ground of thanksgiving, is a real feature of his inner life.
narratives.variation_note: Within Psalm 66's cluster, this reading is the answered climax: prayer recalled as heard and attended, distinct from the crying with the mouth (v17) and the acceptance-focused v20.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is prayer (tefillah) — 'he has not rejected my prayer' (sense), read as action (type). The psalmist bears it (bearer), oriented outward to God (locus external:god), its target God. The operation is to pray, here the prayer God received and did not turn away; its coupling is the prayer whose acceptance grounds the closing blessing. No source (present:false) is named as an inner origin; no seat (none) locates it; manner is none; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — the acceptance sits in the operation as assurance, not a separately booked effect. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v20 'because he has not rejected my prayer.'
narratives.story: The testimony ends on relief: God has not rejected his prayer. Where the earlier lines say God heard, this one says God did not turn the prayer away — the assurance that seals everything and grounds his final blessing of God. The passage does not measure the prayer; the point is simply that it was received. That accepted prayer, proof of God's steadfast love, is a real feature of his inner life.
narratives.variation_note: The closing member of Psalm 66's cluster: the accent here is acceptance — God did not reject the prayer — sealing the testimony, as against the 'attended' focus of v19 and the spoken cry of v17.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is crying out or calling (qara) — 'weary with my crying out' (sense), read as action (type). The psalmist bears it (bearer), oriented outward to God (locus external:god), its target God. The operation is the ceaseless calling to God, and here a seat is given — the throat — with the manner until the throat is parched: crying that has worn the man out, the voice of one in deep waters calling until his throat fails. Its coupling is with weariness and waiting. No source (present:false) names an inner origin; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — pointedly, no answering effect is booked, so the crying wears on toward exhaustion without a recorded reply. No prohibition attaches. Role marks it a characteristic. Grounding: v3 'weary with my crying out.'
narratives.story: This man has cried out to God so long that he is worn out — his throat is dry and cracked from calling. Sunk in deep waters, he keeps shouting upward until his voice fails him, waiting and exhausted. And there is a hard silence here: no answer is recorded to meet all that crying. The passage does not soften it; it simply shows the calling ground down to weariness. That exhausted, unanswered crying is reported honestly as a real movement of his inner life.

narratives.narrative: The characteristic is prayer (tefillah) — 'my prayer is to you, O LORD' (sense), read as action (type). The psalmist bears it (bearer), oriented outward to God (locus external:god), its target the LORD at an acceptable time. The operation is to pray — the turn from the scoffers' songs to God; its source is resting on God's steadfast love and saving faithfulness (v13), and its manner is appealing to that abundant steadfast love. Its coupling is none, the prayer standing alone as his one recourse amid drowning and reproach. No seat (none) locates it; intensity, specifier and effect are unrecorded — no graded force, no booked result, the appeal grounded in God's character. No prohibition attaches.
